characters: Dufie: a cheerful seven-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat braided plaits tied with yellow ribbons, wearing a sunny amber blouse, denim skirt, and brown sandals.
Kpakpo: her wide-eyed four-year-old little brother with short curly hair, wearing a sky-blue T-shirt, khaki shorts, and sandals.

narrationPlan.voice: A bright big-sister voice for Dufie; a small curious voice for Kpakpo
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and bright, slowing for the explanations (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A light xylophone, rising in the morning and softer at noon (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Children in many Ghanaian schools learn about shadows in Integrated Science. The story uses a compound yard and a hand torch that many children know.
The story keeps eye safety in view by reminding readers that Dufie never looks straight at the sun.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check that near noon the shadows are shortest in the area where the story is read (they are very short in the tropics).
Check that the idea “a leaf makes a lighter shadow” is clear for young children.

teacherGuide.overview: A first look at how shadows are made. It teaches that a shadow needs light and an object that blocks it, and that the length of a shadow changes during the day. Activity: trace a shadow in the morning, at noon, and in the afternoon.
learningGoals: Say how a shadow is made.
Say when shadows are longest and shortest.
Test which objects make dark, light, or almost no shadows.
beforeReading: Ask: where have you seen your shadow? Step outside safely and look at it on the ground.
whileReading: Hold up a hand in front of a torch to show how a shadow forms.
afterReading: Trace a shadow with chalk three times a day with an adult watching.
Test five objects in the sunlight and sort them: dark shadow, lighter shadow, or almost no shadow.
discussion: Why is there no shadow in a completely dark room?
Why is your shadow long in the morning and short at noon?
reflection: What did you learn today that you can teach someone at home?

support: Use a torch and a hand against a plain wall so children can see the shadow clearly.
stretch: Predict where the shadow will fall in the afternoon and check it later.

culturalNotes: Children in many Ghanaian schools learn about shadows in Integrated Science. The story uses a compound yard and a hand torch that many children know.
The story keeps eye safety in view by reminding readers that Dufie never looks straight at the sun.
localiseThis: Use a familiar compound yard, shade tree, or school block for the shadow walk.
Remind children never to look straight at the sun.

factCheck.claim: Shadows are longest in the morning and late afternoon and shortest near noon.
factCheck.explanation: When the sun is low in the sky, blocked light casts a long shadow; when the sun is high overhead near midday, the shadow falls closely beneath the object.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Ghana Primary Integrated Science Curriculum (Light and Shadows)
